screens.title: Inheritance with the is keyword
screens.narratorSegment: Inheritance in Solidity lets a derived contract adopt public and internal members from a base contract through the is keyword. That means state variables and functions declared in the base become available in the child, enabling reuse and centralization of common logic. For example, an Ownable base contract defines an owner address and an onlyOwner modifier. Any contract that declares is Ownable gains that owner state and can protect functions with onlyOwner rather than reimplementing ownership checks. A common misconception is that private members are inherited — they are not. Private fields remain inaccessible to derived contracts, so use internal if children need direct access. Multiple inheritance is allowed, so you may inherit from several bases, but be mindful of name conflicts and the linearized inheritance order. A concrete example: MyContract is Ownable will automatically call Ownable's parameterless constructor and expose owner; you can then write setValue guarded by onlyOwner so only the owner can change state. Takeaway: use inheritance to reduce duplication, but design visibility intentionally and prefer modifiers in a base contract to standardize access control. How will you structure an ownership A P I so derived contracts remain minimal and safe?

keyIdea.title: Definition — Inheritance
keyIdea.text: Use is to let a derived contract inherit public and internal members from a base contract, enabling code reuse and shared access control.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Inheritance with is
Core Concept

Inheritance via is

Derived contracts adopt public and internal members from base contracts. Use inheritance to centralize logic like ownership and modifiers.

// Base
contract Ownable {
  address public owner;
  constructor() { owner = msg.sender; }
  modifier onlyOwner() { require(msg.sender == owner, "Caller is not the owner"); _; }
}

// Derived
contract MyContract is Ownable {
  uint256 public value;
  constructor(uint256 _initialValue) { value = _initialValue; }
  function setValue(uint256 _newValue) public onlyOwner { value = _newValue; }
}
How it works
  • Derived contracts gain public and internal state and functions from the base.
  • Private members are not inherited; use internal when children need access.
  • Modifiers like onlyOwner standardize access control across many contracts.
  • Multiple inheritance is supported, but follow the linearization rules to avoid ambiguity.
Concrete example
MyContract is Ownable inherits owner and onlyOwner. Calling setValue by a non-owner will revert because onlyOwner requires the caller to match owner.
Key Takeaway

is enables safe reuse; design visibility and modifiers in the base to keep derived contracts small and auditable.

screens.title: Multiple inheritance and execution order
screens.narratorSegment: Solidity supports multiple inheritance, but understanding the order in which constructors and overrides run is essential. When a contract inherits from multiple bases using is BaseA, BaseB, the linearized order determines which base constructors are called and in what sequence. The compiler resolves the most base contracts first, then proceeds toward the most derived. Practically this means that if both bases have constructors that take arguments, the derived contract must explicitly call those constructors in its header. A common concrete mistake is to leave out a required base constructor call when a base requires parameters; that will fail compilation or leave state uninitialized. Another frequent pitfall is forgetting to specify override when multiple bases declare the same virtual function. For example, if BaseA and BaseB both declare function foo() virtual, the derived contract must implement foo() with override(BaseA, BaseB). To summarize, when composing several base contracts: declare them left-to-right, explicitly call constructors with arguments, and use override lists for conflicting functions. A final reflection: consider whether you need multiple inheritance or whether composition and interfaces might produce a simpler, less error-prone design.

keyIdea.title: Process — multiple inheritance
keyIdea.text: Linearization controls constructor order and override resolution; call base constructors explicitly when arguments are required.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Multiple inheritance
Process Flow

Constructor & override order

Step-by-step
  1. List bases in the is clause: contract D is A, B { ... }
  2. Compiler determines linearized order from most base to most derived.
  3. Base constructors run first; derived runs last.
  4. If base constructors require args, call them explicitly in the derived constructor.
  5. When overriding functions from multiple bases, use override(BaseA, BaseB).
Common mistake
Neglecting to call a base constructor with required parameters leaves base state at defaults and causes subtle bugs or compilation errors.
Example
contract BaseA { constructor(uint x) { /*...*/ } }
contract BaseB { constructor(uint y) { /*...*/ } }
contract Derived is BaseA, BaseB {
  constructor(uint x, uint y) BaseA(x) BaseB(y) { }
}

screens.title: Constructor chaining
screens.narratorSegment: Constructor chaining ensures that every base contract that requires initialization is properly called when a derived contract is deployed. If a base contract's constructor has no parameters, it is called implicitly. If it requires arguments, the derived contract must call it explicitly in its constructor header using BaseName(arg1, arg2). The overall execution order follows inheritance linearization: the most base constructors run first, then progressively more derived constructors run, and finally the derived contract's body executes. A concrete scenario from the chapter shows another common pattern: AccessControl defines an owner in its constructor, and ManagedToken relies on that owner for minting rights. If you fail to call a base constructor correctly, base state such as owner may remain the default address, causing access checks to fail unexpectedly. Another misconception is thinking that constructor chaining happens automatically with arguments — it does not. Always inspect base constructors and ensure required parameters are forwarded. Key takeaway: constructor chaining is the single point where base state is established; plan constructor signatures so derived contracts can initialize all bases clearly. Constructor chaining means explicitly call base constructors with arguments when required; execution goes from the most base to the most derived.. In practical terms, how and when base constructors run during deployment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Explicitly call base constructors with arguments when required; execution goes from the most base to the most derived.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Constructor chaining
Definition

Constructor chaining

When deploying a derived contract, base constructors must be executed so base state is initialized. Call bases explicitly when they accept parameters; otherwise the implicit call will apply only if there are no arguments.
contract Base { constructor(uint n) { /* set base */ } }
contract Derived is Base {
  constructor(uint n) Base(n) { /* derived init */ }
}
Why it matters

Missing a base constructor call can leave critical state like owner unset and break access control, tests, and security assumptions.

Common mistake

Assuming base constructors with parameters will be called implicitly. Always forward required arguments explicitly in the derived constructor signature.

keyIdea.text: AccessControl defines owner and onlyOwner; ManagedToken inherits that behavior to implement minting and transfers protected by ownership.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Ownable / ManagedToken
Code Walkthrough

AccessControl → ManagedToken

// Base contract for basic ownership
contract AccessControl {
  address public owner;
  event OwnershipTransferred(address indexed previousOwner, address indexed newOwner);
  constructor() { owner = msg.sender; }
  modifier onlyOwner() { require(msg.sender == owner, "Caller is not the owner"); _; }
  function transferOwnership(address _newOwner) public onlyOwner { require(_newOwner != address(0)); owner = _newOwner; emit OwnershipTransferred(msg.sender, _newOwner); }
}

// Derived contract
contract ManagedToken is AccessControl {
  string public name; string public symbol; uint256 public totalSupply; mapping(address => uint256) public balances;
  constructor(string memory _name, string memory _symbol) { name = _name; symbol = _symbol; }
  function mint(address _to, uint256 _amount) public onlyOwner { totalSupply += _amount; balances[_to] += _amount; }
}
Runtime scenario
Deploy ManagedToken on Remix using JavaScript VM with constructor args "MyToken","MTK". The deployer is owner and can mint. Switching accounts to a non-owner and calling mint should revert.
Misconception
Token transfer does not change contract ownership. transfer updates balances; transferOwnership updates who can call onlyOwner functions.
Key Takeaway

Use the base contract to centralize access control and keep derived contracts focused on domain logic like minting and transfers.

screens.title: Abstract contracts
screens.narratorSegment: An abstract contract contains one or more functions declared without implementation. It cannot be deployed on its own; instead, another contract must inherit from it and implement every unimplemented function. Abstract contracts are useful when you want to define a shared blueprint that enforces a shape of behavior while still providing concrete helpers. For instance, a PaymentProcessor abstract contract can expose an immutable processorAddress, a constructor to set it, and an abstract function processPayment(address, amount) that derived contracts must implement. The concrete EthereumPaymentProcessor then overrides processPayment and provides the actual logic for sending Ether or calling another system. A common misconception is confusing abstract contracts with interfaces. Abstract contracts may have state variables, a constructor, and concrete helper functions in addition to abstract functions; interfaces cannot. Use abstract contracts when you need shared storage or helper implementations alongside abstract members. The learning takeaway: choose abstract contracts to provide a reusable mix of state, helpers, and required functions while forcing derived contracts to implement key behaviors. Abstract contracts means a contract with at least one unimplemented function that acts as a blueprint; it can include state, constructors, and helper functions.. In practical terms, blueprints with unimplemented functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Abstract Contracts
Definition

Abstract contract

An abstract contract defines one or more functions without bodies and may include state and concrete helper methods. It cannot be deployed until a derived contract implements its abstract functions.

abstract contract PaymentProcessor {
  address public immutable processorAddress;
  constructor(address _processor) { processorAddress = _processor; }
  function processPayment(address _to, uint256 _amount) public virtual returns (bool);
  function getProcessorAddress() public view returns (address) { return processorAddress; }
}
Concrete implementation
EthereumPaymentProcessor implements processPayment and therefore becomes a deployable contract. Abstract contracts are useful when you need shared state or helper code plus an enforced API.
Misconception
Abstract contracts are not the same as interfaces: they can include constructors, state, and concrete methods.
Key Takeaway

Use abstract contracts to enforce a blueprint while supplying shared state or helper implementations to derived contracts.

screens.title: Interfaces and external interaction (IERC20)
screens.narratorSegment: Interfaces define a contract's external A P I with function signatures only, no state and no constructors. This simplicity is deliberate: it guarantees that any contract implementing the interface exposes those functions externally, so your contract can interact without knowing internal details. A common example is an ERC-20-style interface that declares totalSupply, balanceOf, transfer, and transferFrom as external functions. In practice you cast a known address to the interface type and call functions directly. For example, MyTokenConsumer stores an IERC20 token reference initialized by passing the token's address to the constructor. Then getTokenBalance calls token. balanceOf(user) and sendTokens calls token. transfer(recipient, amount). This pattern enables interoperability across different token implementations. A frequent misconception is trying to add state or concrete functions to an interface; that will fail compilation. Use interfaces when you only need to know and call external behavior; prefer abstract contracts when you also need shared storage or helper methods. Key takeaway: casting to an interface is a safe, simple way to call external contracts that conform to a known A P I. Interfaces and external interaction (IERC20) means define external function signatures to call any compatible contract by casting its address to the interface type.. In practical terms, how to call another contract through an interface. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Define external function signatures to call any compatible contract by casting its address to the interface type.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Interfaces (IERC20)
Architecture

Calling external contracts

Cast a deployed contract address to an interface type so you can call its external functions by signature without access to its code.
interface IERC20 {
  function totalSupply() external view returns (uint256);
  function balanceOf(address account) external view returns (uint256);
  function transfer(address recipient, uint256 amount) external returns (bool);
}

contract MyTokenConsumer {
  IERC20 public token;
  constructor(address _tokenAddress) { token = IERC20(_tokenAddress); }
  function getTokenBalance(address _user) public view returns (uint256) { return token.balanceOf(_user); }
  function sendTokens(address _recipient, uint256 _amount) public returns (bool) { return token.transfer(_recipient, _amount); }
}
Why use interfaces
They allow interaction with deployed contracts that follow a standard API, fostering interoperability without sharing implementation details.

Libraries

screens.title: Abstract contract vs interface
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between an abstract contract and an interface is a design decision driven by whether you need shared state or just a signature. Interfaces contain only external function signatures, cannot have state variables or constructors, and cannot define modifiers. They are ideal when you only need to call external functions on a deployed contract, for example calling balanceOf and transfer on an ERC-20 token. Abstract contracts, by contrast, can include state, a constructor, concrete helper methods, and abstract functions that derived contracts must implement. Use an abstract contract when you want to provide shared storage or utility functions while still forcing derived contracts to implement core behavior. A common misconception is to treat interfaces as a lighter-weight abstract contract; interfaces are stricter and compile-time enforced to be signatures only. Example: define IERC20 as an interface to call token functions from a consumer contract. If you need a blueprint with shared processorAddress and helper methods, use an abstract PaymentProcessor. Key takeaway: prefer interfaces for external APIs and abstract contracts when you also require shared state or helper implementations. Comparison

Abstract contract vs Interface

Interface
  • Only external function signatures.
  • No state, constructors, or modifiers.
  • Best for calling external contracts and enforcing API compatibility.
Abstract contract

screens.title: Hands-on: ManagedToken in Remix
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough guides you through implementing and testing the ManagedToken example in Remix. screens.title: Quiz walkthrough and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Let's analyze the assessment question about interacting with an ERC-721 contract: which feature defines external functions you need without implementation? The correct choice is an interface. An interface specifies only external function signatures and lets your contract call those functions by casting an address to the interface type. Why not inheritance? Inheriting from the ERC-721 would mean your contract becomes an ERC-721 itself, which is not what you want when only calling an existing contract. An abstract contract could work but is heavier: it allows state and constructors and is not necessary when you only need to declare external functions. A library is for stateless utilities and not suitable for defining external contract APIs. Next, consider a second example about base constructor arguments not being called: if a base has a constructor requiring arguments and you do not call it explicitly in the derived constructor, base state remains default. This explains why baseValue would be zero and how to fix it by calling Base(_val1) from the derived constructor. Finally, review common mistakes: forgetting override will fail compilation in Solidity 0.6.0+; visibility mistakes, such as expecting private to be inherited, will break access. Reflect: when could an abstract contract be preferable to an interface for your design?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how Solidity lets you reuse code, enforce a contract's external A P I, and interact with other deployed contracts safely. We will use inheritance with the is keyword to adopt state and behavior from base contracts, and we will examine constructor chaining so that base state is reliably initialized when a derived contract is deployed. You will see abstract contracts that define unimplemented functions as blueprints, and interfaces that describe external APIs like ERC-20 without implementation or state. We'll also briefly cover libraries for stateless, reusable logic. A concrete example you will study is the Ownable pattern, where multiple contracts can share an owner address and an onlyOwner modifier. You'll also practice with an AccessControl and ManagedToken pair in a hands-on walkthrough. As you progress, notice common pitfalls: forgetting override, missing constructor arguments, and attempting state inside an interface. By the end you'll understand when to choose inheritance, an abstract contract, an interface, or a library, and how these choices affect interoperability and safety.

In this first objectives slide we set practical goals. You will implement contract inheritance using the is keyword so derived contracts can reuse state variables and functions. This matters because inheritance reduces duplication and centralizes common logic such as an owner address or access modifier. You will also understand constructor chaining: how base constructors run and how to call them explicitly when they require arguments. Knowing constructor chaining prevents uninitialized base state and compilation errors. You will differentiate abstract contracts and concrete contracts: abstract contracts contain at least one function without an implementation and therefore cannot be deployed until a derived contract implements those functions. Finally, you will define and implement interfaces to enforce contract structure and allow interaction with external contracts using agreed function signatures. Each objective maps to a verified competency milestone so you can confirm the skill.

This second objectives slide focuses on applying the concepts. You will implement an AccessControl base contract and a ManagedToken derived contract to practice constructor chaining and inherited modifiers in a live environment. This exercise matters because ownership and access control are common patterns that must be correct to avoid security issues. You will also practice casting an address to an interface type and calling external functions like balanceOf and transfer to observe how a consumer interacts with an ERC-20-style A P I. Additionally, you will briefly explain libraries and when to favor a library for stateless utilities. Finally, you will identify common mistakes such as forgetting override or attempting state inside an interface so you can recognize and fix compilation errors quickly. Each objective links to a milestone so you can verify the competency after the hands-on steps.

Inheritance in Solidity lets a derived contract adopt public and internal members from a base contract through the is keyword. That means state variables and functions declared in the base become available in the child, enabling reuse and centralization of common logic. For example, an Ownable base contract defines an owner address and an onlyOwner modifier. Any contract that declares is Ownable gains that owner state and can protect functions with onlyOwner rather than reimplementing ownership checks. A common misconception is that private members are inherited — they are not. Private fields remain inaccessible to derived contracts, so use internal if children need direct access. Multiple inheritance is allowed, so you may inherit from several bases, but be mindful of name conflicts and the linearized inheritance order. A concrete example: MyContract is Ownable will automatically call Ownable's parameterless constructor and expose owner; you can then write setValue guarded by onlyOwner so only the owner can change state. Takeaway: use inheritance to reduce duplication, but design visibility intentionally and prefer modifiers in a base contract to standardize access control. How will you structure an ownership A P I so derived contracts remain minimal and safe?

Solidity supports multiple inheritance, but understanding the order in which constructors and overrides run is essential. When a contract inherits from multiple bases using is BaseA, BaseB, the linearized order determines which base constructors are called and in what sequence. The compiler resolves the most base contracts first, then proceeds toward the most derived. Practically this means that if both bases have constructors that take arguments, the derived contract must explicitly call those constructors in its header. A common concrete mistake is to leave out a required base constructor call when a base requires parameters; that will fail compilation or leave state uninitialized. Another frequent pitfall is forgetting to specify override when multiple bases declare the same virtual function. For example, if BaseA and BaseB both declare function foo() virtual, the derived contract must implement foo() with override(BaseA, BaseB). To summarize, when composing several base contracts: declare them left-to-right, explicitly call constructors with arguments, and use override lists for conflicting functions. A final reflection: consider whether you need multiple inheritance or whether composition and interfaces might produce a simpler, less error-prone design.

Constructor chaining ensures that every base contract that requires initialization is properly called when a derived contract is deployed. If a base contract's constructor has no parameters, it is called implicitly. If it requires arguments, the derived contract must call it explicitly in its constructor header using BaseName(arg1, arg2). The overall execution order follows inheritance linearization: the most base constructors run first, then progressively more derived constructors run, and finally the derived contract's body executes. A concrete scenario from the chapter shows another common pattern: AccessControl defines an owner in its constructor, and ManagedToken relies on that owner for minting rights. If you fail to call a base constructor correctly, base state such as owner may remain the default address, causing access checks to fail unexpectedly. Another misconception is thinking that constructor chaining happens automatically with arguments — it does not. Always inspect base constructors and ensure required parameters are forwarded. Key takeaway: constructor chaining is the single point where base state is established; plan constructor signatures so derived contracts can initialize all bases clearly. Constructor chaining means explicitly call base constructors with arguments when required; execution goes from the most base to the most derived.. In practical terms, how and when base constructors run during deployment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the AccessControl and ManagedToken pair to make the concepts concrete. AccessControl defines an owner, an OwnershipTransferred event, a constructor that sets owner to the deployer, and an onlyOwner modifier that protects functions. ManagedToken inherits AccessControl and defines name, symbol, totalSupply, and balances. Its constructor initializes name and symbol while AccessControl's parameterless constructor runs implicitly. The mint function is guarded by onlyOwner so only the deployer can mint new tokens. Transfer and transferOwnership show how state changes are emitted via events. When you deploy ManagedToken in Remix with arguments like MyToken and MTK, the deployer becomes owner. Interact by minting as that account and verifying balances; switching accounts and calling mint from a non-owner will revert. A misconception learners often have is expecting ownership to change automatically on transfer; ownership and token transfers are separate: transfer changes balances while transferOwnership changes the owner used by onlyOwner. An abstract contract contains one or more functions declared without implementation. It cannot be deployed on its own; instead, another contract must inherit from it and implement every unimplemented function. Abstract contracts are useful when you want to define a shared blueprint that enforces a shape of behavior while still providing concrete helpers. For instance, a PaymentProcessor abstract contract can expose an immutable processorAddress, a constructor to set it, and an abstract function processPayment(address, amount) that derived contracts must implement. The concrete EthereumPaymentProcessor then overrides processPayment and provides the actual logic for sending Ether or calling another system. A common misconception is confusing abstract contracts with interfaces. Abstract contracts may have state variables, a constructor, and concrete helper functions in addition to abstract functions; interfaces cannot. Use abstract contracts when you need shared storage or helper implementations alongside abstract members. The learning takeaway: choose abstract contracts to provide a reusable mix of state, helpers, and required functions while forcing derived contracts to implement key behaviors. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Interfaces define a contract's external A P I with function signatures only, no state and no constructors. This simplicity is deliberate: it guarantees that any contract implementing the interface exposes those functions externally, so your contract can interact without knowing internal details. A common example is an ERC-20-style interface that declares totalSupply, balanceOf, transfer, and transferFrom as external functions. In practice you cast a known address to the interface type and call functions directly. For example, MyTokenConsumer stores an IERC20 token reference initialized by passing the token's address to the constructor. Let's analyze the assessment question about interacting with an ERC-721 contract: which feature defines external functions you need without implementation? The correct choice is an interface. An interface specifies only external function signatures and lets your contract call those functions by casting an address to the interface type. Why not inheritance? Summarizing the essentials: Inheritance with the is keyword lets derived contracts reuse public and internal state and functions; remember private is not inherited and use internal for child access. Interfaces define only external function signatures and allow contracts to call deployed systems like tokens by casting an address to the interface type; they cannot have state or constructors. Abstract contracts serve as blueprints that can include state, constructors, and helper methods but require derived contracts to implement unimplemented functions before deployment. These three patterns cover the main choices you will make when structuring contracts: reuse implementation in bases, define external APIs as interfaces, or combine both approaches using abstract contracts when shared state and helper code are needed.
